In this interview with ABIODUN ADEWALE, the Lagos State governorship candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, Funso Doherty, talks about his fitness routine, admiration for Nigeria’s elite athletes and plans to harness sports development through schools and communities As someone who has spent most of his career in the corporate world and is now in politics, what do you do for fitness, and how do you ensure you strike a work-fitness balance? My primary fitness activity is running, and I have been doing it for 25 years. I tend to run about three or four times a week, covering at least five or six kilometres. Why I started running because I used to play squash when I was in school, but when I started working, it became a bit difficult to keep up with it because you would have to look for a partner and find a time that works for both of you to go to the squash court. So, as a busy young man, I wasn’t playing or doing anything sporty. That was why I switched to running because, with that, you only need your shoes and essentials. I also do cycling. Ideally, I like to run in the evenings because I am a bit of a morning person. I would be in very early, as early as 6:30 am, so I can leave the office by 5pm and have some time for running. I found a way to manage it because I prioritised it. If you have to watch any sport on TV or at the stadium, what would it be? Occasionally, I may watch athletics, especially when it’s the World Championships or Olympics. I am a big fan of athletics, so I tend to keep up with their major events, and of course, I am almost certain that a Nigerian would be in action. I am not a big football person, but if Nigeria is playing, I usually follow it out of patriotism. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources What’s your impression of some of our biggest athletics exports, like Chioma Ajunwa, Tobi Amusan, Ese Brume, Soji Fasuba and others? When you see somebody who is operating at championship or Olympic level, they are at the peak of a very large pyramid. They have worked to reach that level, so I have nothing but the greatest respect for athletes who have shown the commitment and discipline to be out there. We should continue to highlight them as role models for those coming behind them. When you talk about respect for these kinds of athletes, how do you integrate upcoming ones into your plans as a governorship candidate in Lagos State? If you went to the stadium, you would see there are active communities doing almost every sport and activity you can think of. There is dance, skating, football, volleyball, karate, boxing, and that shows there is a whole sense of community that can be built around sports. These are people engaging in something wholesome and healthy. So, a sports programme is an important part of what we are pursuing. For us, the link between that is the schools and communities, which will be strengthened tremendously. We will ensure that the nexus between them is strong because they are pillars for strengthening the social fabric. If well managed and properly harnessed, we will produce athletes who will take the world by storm, like Chioma Ajunwa and Tobi Amusan, because we have the talent. With the right system, resources and organisation, it can be a way to build stronger values in our society. In communities, we do have sports fields, and we need to do more to prioritise these facilities and ensure that we have programmes that keep them running. The greatest asset that we have is our people, and the greatest number are the youth. If you didn’t go into the corporate world, did you ever fancy being a footballer or athlete? No. Maybe I was too realistic about my own abilities, and I went to look for where I was gifted to contribute, and that is what I am doing. Abiodun Adewale Abiodun, who reports Sports for PUNCH, covers different tiers of the Nigerian football league, the national teams, as well as cricket, in the last six years
